entries.title: Trump Tests the Definition of Insider Trading
entries.summary: A new Truth Social subscription service is another way for the president to profit from his office.
entries.content:
A new Truth Social subscription service is another way for the president to profit from his office.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

For Donald Trump, social media is a fundamental component of the presidency. He shares his thoughts freely and constantly; world-shaking announcements that other presidents might have reserved for prime-time speeches, he posts online.

Trump Media and Technology Group, the company that controls Truth Social and is majority-owned by the president, is now selling speedy access to those posts through a service called Truth API. Launched this weekend, it provides users a raw feed of “market-moving” posts from the “highest-ranking Truth Social accounts”—the top one being Trump’s, which has 13 million followers. Typically, social-media users encounter split-second lag times before being notified about new posts; Truth API purports to minimize delays. It’s aimed at investment firms that can afford the subscription price (Trump Media has not publicized the cost, but The Wall Street Journal and others have reported that it’s up to $100,000 a month), and promises traders an advantage over their competitors. It also gives Trump Media a way to capitalize directly on the president’s words—and gives Trump another way to capitalize on the nation’s highest office.

The initial press release for Truth API made no mention of the president’s posts. But Truth Social was created primarily as a vehicle for Trump’s own commentary after he was booted off Twitter in 2021 following the January 6 riot. New accounts on the website automatically follow Trump, as well as Donald Trump Jr. and many others. (Trump Media declined to answer my questions, and the White House denied that Truth API creates conflicts of interest for the president.)

The value of the new service hinges on the fact that Trump’s statements move markets. This president has a habit of sharing new policies on social media before the White House has had a chance to release an official statement. He has used Truth Social to make adjustments to tariff rules, announce military actions, and telegraph future plans for foreign interventions. (Many observers have also pointed out that he tends to wait until after trading hours to share news that might have an undesirable effect on markets, as has been the case throughout the Iran war.)

The president’s comments portend stock-market shifts in lower-stakes situations too. One recent example: Trump told the public to “go out and buy” a Dell computer at least four times this year. He began doing this on February 19, about a week after he purchased at least $1 million worth of Dell stock. The last time Trump dropped this line, at the White House in July, the share price immediately climbed by almost 8 percent. Maybe the president just really likes Dell computers—or maybe he really likes the company’s CEO, Michael Dell, who, along with his wife, pledged to donate more than $6 billion to the administration’s new child-savings-account program. The president encouraged people to buy in, and shareholders made money.

Trump Media has said that Truth API data will be delivered in “milliseconds,” providing what they say is the “fastest access” to these posts. Critics argue that this gives certain traders an unfair, or even illegal, leg up: Senators Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff wrote a letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission last week demanding an investigation into the service. The letter suggests that, because the service offers access to market-moving posts before most people have had a chance to see it, it could potentially violate insider-trading laws, which ban trades based on nonpublic information.

But most of the experts I spoke with questioned this logic. Existing securities laws don’t fit this situation perfectly. Trump Media told The Wall Street Journal that Truth Social posts will continue to be publicly viewable at the same time for all users, whether they pay for Truth API or not. Those who subscribe will be notified slightly before the rest of us, but the posts themselves won’t be delayed or hidden—which could make it hard to argue that the information contained within them isn’t actually public. And Trump Media didn’t invent the concept of high-speed data feeds for institutional traders. As Stephen Bainbridge, a professor at UCLA Law, has pointed out, today’s stock exchanges already sell similar products, which are broadly considered legal.

Some of the legal scholars I interviewed observed that because this situation is unprecedented, the law may simply not have caught up. The SEC could potentially play a role in investigating Trump Media, but the agency, now under the aegis of Trump’s handpicked chair, Paul Atkins, has not commented on Warren and Schiff’s letter. (A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment for this story.) When I asked Jonathan Macey, a professor at Yale Law, what he thought of Warren and Schiff’s letter, he told me that they were essentially asking the fox to come check on the henhouse.

Truth API is a clear attempt to create a new revenue stream for a struggling company—its CEO, former Representative Devin Nunes, stepped down earlier this year after overseeing hundreds of millions of dollars in losses during his tenure. It’s also yet another way for Trump to make money from the office of the presidency. Trump reported that he earned more than $2.2 billion last year, much of which came from cryptocurrency tokens and investments. No other president has ever come close to generating this much personal wealth while in office. Now he stands to profit from something more straightforward: unmediated access to his own thoughts.

Related:

Here are three new stories from The Atlantic:

Today’s News

  • The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general. The nomination now heads to a vote in the full Senate.
  • President Trump met with U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro at the White House after publicly criticizing her for dropping vandalism charges related to damage at the Reflecting Pool. Pirro was not fired and did not resign following the meeting, according to people familiar with the matter.
  • Representative Max Miller’s attorney apologized after the Ohio Republican publicly shared unredacted court documents that included a “sensitive” image of his young daughter, saying that the photo was inadvertently released. Miller is facing domestic-abuse allegations, which he has denied, from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who is also the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio.

Evening Read

The Catholic Church’s New Schism

By Luis Parrales

At an open-air Mass in Écône, Switzerland, before a crowd of about 16,000 people, four priests became bishops last month. The men professed their fidelity to tradition against “heretics, schismatics, and those who rebel against our Holy Father.” They did so knowing full well that, in becoming bishops, they lacked something the Catholic Church deems essential: permission from the pope.

entries.title: Trump’s Irrationality Is Dangerous
entries.summary: The president’s recent rant is a sign of serious dysfunction in the Oval Office.
entries.content:
The president’s recent rant is a sign of serious dysfunction in the Oval Office.

Many Americans—and much of the rest of the world—have become inured to Donald Trump’s strange rants. When he shouts about sharks, when he drones on about his brilliant uncle, when he casually ponders violating the Constitution, his supporters try to dress his statements up as some kind of strategy: He’s not lost touch with reality, you see. He’s doing the weave, or he’s owning the libs. He’s fighting the fake news and flooding the zone. He knows what he’s doing.

These excuses have never really held much water. But his rant yesterday about the Reflecting Pool (speaking of things that don’t hold water) was a warning that the president has encased himself in the hard amber of irrationality that inevitably surrounds authoritarian leaders. He has become detached from reality—and that detachment is extremely dangerous.

The Reflecting Pool mess is different from other Trump obsessions because it reveals just how immune to evidence and logic his beliefs have become, even when a trusted lieutenant wheels an entire box of supporting evidence into the Oval Office. In Trump’s world, nothing is ever innocent. If something went wrong, the fault must lie with Americans conspiring against him, not with a contractor who did shabby work. And so the boss put out the order: Find the criminals who destroyed my lovely pool.

The task of prosecuting this inane case fell to Jeanine Pirro, who has known Trump for more than three decades. She has long been one of his most loyal defenders on Fox News, and she was his personal choice for the job of U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia after the failed nomination of Ed Martin. She dutifully charged multiple people with vandalizing the Reflecting Pool, including the Olympic athlete David Hearn. But last week, she moved to drop the case after admitting that the pool’s condition was “the result of a botched installation” and not of criminal activity. Trump immediately turned on her. In a Truth Social post after Pirro’s filing, Trump said he disagreed “100%” with his old friend. “I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM.”

This outburst, however, was merely a warm-up for a nearly 10-minute performance yesterday afternoon in the Oval Office that went well beyond Trump’s usual whining. Pirro, he said, “choked” under pressure from the court. She “made a mistake. It was vandalism.” He continued:

One of the things was, the Reflecting Pool hasn’t worked since 1922, because it always leaked. It always leaked from 1922. You know, it’s the largest, longest pool ever, all that. The concept is beautiful, but it always leaked because of the size, because of maintenance, whatever. But it was built in 1922, and from the day it was built, it was—it leaked. Biden spent $58 million. Barack Hussein Obama spent much more than that. He said, “I have an idea. Let’s take the river from, let’s take the water from the Potomac.” So they took the water from the Potomac, and it was putrid. It was putrid. It was a disaster. Biden was a disaster.

But how did Trump know that Pirro was wrong and he was right? “We have photographs or tapes,” he said, “like moving cameras, right? We have them where people are on the side, cutting it with a box knife.” Trump then admitted that he wasn’t “thrilled” with the work the contractor did, but “in addition, there was vandalism.” He complained about some damage to the grass nearby, but then came back to the pool, where “they took knives or cutters, and they cut the material—it’s material. And they put their hands and they pulled it.”

Pirro undermined all of this in a lengthy filing to the court that accompanied her request to withdraw the case. Perhaps in an earlier time, when Trump appeared more amenable to listening to the advice of friends and trusted advisers, he might have been satisfied with the harassment of his opponents. As the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan wrote in their recent book on Trump, he admitted that he wanted charges filed just to harass perceived enemies such as New York Attorney General Letitia James, even if the charges were unlikely to stick. “I want to make her life miserable,” they quote him as saying to an adviser.

But Trump has now passed from being a stubborn narcissist to a cocooned authoritarian. Political scientists since World War II have studied the problem of “irrational” leaders, people in positions of power who seem unable to accept any version of reality that conflicts with their assumptions. Irrational, in this sense, does not mean “stupid,” or “incompetent,” or “psychotic.” It refers more specifically to leaders who have become so trapped by their own self-regard, so isolated from the outside world, so imprisoned within their own sense of infallibility that they refuse to consider any arguments or information that conflicts with their beliefs.

Trump reportedly relishes being compared to some of the great dictators of the past, but he apparently does not comprehend how their stories are also warnings. Joseph Stalin was so certain he had outfoxed the Nazis that he fell into catatonic denial for several days after the Germans attacked in 1941. Saddam Hussein refused to believe that American troops were crossing into Iraq, even as tanks rumbled toward Baghdad. Nicolae Ceaușescu of Romania was one of many leaders throughout history who refused to believe that he was about to be deposed, despite troops advancing on their palace. (He and his wife died shouting orders at their firing squad.)

Trump’s detachment from reality is sometimes amusing and often alarming, but the price of his irrationality until now has been mostly economic and reputational (or, in the case of the Reflecting Pool, aesthetic, now that the cases against innocent Americans have been dropped). His belief in tariffs, for example, is a flatly irrational attachment to a tool that has been proven, over and over, to harm Americans. Likewise, his fixation on NATO has undermined decades of careful diplomacy and weakened the strongest alliance in history.

The war in Iran, however, has shown that Trump’s inability to perceive reality has become truly dangerous. He led the United States into a disastrous conflict because he thought his “gut” was smarter than the advisers who warned him that deposing Iran’s regime was unlikely. He continues to mislead the American people, and perhaps himself, about America’s strategic defeat at the hands of one of its worst enemies. The world economy and the balance of power have been changed, perhaps for many decades to come, because Trump cannot draw links between cause and effect; he does not understand that his actions and the failures that follow are somehow related to each other.

Iran is a disaster, but Trump’s irrationality could create other, even more perilous situations. When the water systems in seven states were recently subjected to cyberattacks, Trump blamed his fellow Americans, despite evidence of foreign involvement. What if America suffers another mass-terror attack, and Trump decides that it, too, is the work of disloyal Americans instead of foreigners? Will his underlings round people up based on such a delusion? Or perhaps Trump, if his party is beaten soundly in the midterms, will make up his mind that such a loss is impossible and call for invalidating the election’s results. He might even inspire his supporters to violence—as he did on January 6, 2021.

More worrisome is the possibility of a military crisis that unfolds quickly and threatens U.S. allies or the United States itself. If Russian President Vladimir Putin decides to test NATO and attacks a member of the alliance, or if China begins to move in the Pacific, could anyone in Trump’s inner circle contradict the president’s presumptions and biases? If, say, Russia or China or other powers go to a heightened state of nuclear alert, Trump would have to make decisions of potentially cataclysmic importance. Would he listen, even to basic information, if it conflicted with his omniscient gut?

Trump has always been notoriously un-briefable, but in his first term, he had people who would try to speak the truth to him. More important, he was capable, at least to some limited degree, of occasionally listening to those assistants. All of that is gone. Trump slamming his old friend Pirro shows that when even the most trusted allies offer him the truth, he won’t accept it.

Trump is not going to have some sudden epiphany about the need for an open and honest policy process. Like other authoritarians before him, the president has retreated, irrevocably, behind the walls of his own Forbidden City of the mind—a place where he is the emperor, his judgment is always right, and his commands must always be obeyed.

entries.title: Now, Thanks to Sam Altman, You Never Have to Speak With Your Kids Again
entries.summary: AI can handle these kinds of pointless interactions.
entries.content:
AI can handle these kinds of pointless interactions.

“cool use case of chatgpt work i heard last night:

connect your family calendars and explain your kids' interests.

every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid's soccer game that afternoon, one kid's upcoming birthday, some news, etc.”

Parents! Are you getting fed up? Throwing away your life interacting with your children when you could be profitmaxxing? When you could be proteinmaxxing? When you could be doing whatever it is that billionaire guy with the repeated infusions of fresh young blood is doing?

Consider: What do children bring to the table, besides sticky fingers? Forget networking! They don’t know anyone. Bluey? That is a cartoon dog. Paw Patrol? Still a cartoon dog, but now it possesses law-enforcement powers.

Besides, kids are fonts of misinformation. Anyone can see that the floor is not lava. That is plainly not a fort. Those are cushions. If you wanted erroneous information presented to you in a confident way, you would be asking ChatGPT. At least it has the decency to grovel. And what can children offer you in return? Magnatiles? A picture of an ape? Wait, that could be something! Oh, never mind. It’s hand-drawn on construction paper.

What a relief that AI can handle all these pointless interactions. It can make a podcast. This offers two advantages: You can avoid talking with your children (this makes it less embarrassing that you do not remember your second child’s name; maybe … Tid?), and it may endear your children to AI, which will come in handy in case it ever does gain sentience.

You’re missing nothing. Kids have no information of value to impart. On the contrary, all they ever do is ask embarrassingly basic, rudimentary questions about the world. “What is gravity?” “Why is the microwave spinning?” “Why do you keep putting on that weird podcast every time we’re in the car?” ENOUGH WITH THE QUESTIONS, TID!

If you make the mistake of listening to your children now, you might be stuck with them in your life forever. Maybe they’ll fall in love and want to tell you about it! Maybe they’ll need a ride home from a party! Maybe they’ll make something they’re proud of and want to show you! And you will have to spend the rest of your life listening to them. Ugh. You might even get invited to their wedding, or be asked to spend time with your grandchildren.

The inefficiency is chilling. It’s so much work for so little reward. All these people, wasting their life going to their children’s soccer games and piano recitals and listening to them tell their interminable stories. What does it all amount to, anyway? Best-case scenario, they will stand up at your funeral and deliver a eulogy saying that you were a “loving, present parent who shaped me into the person I am today”—and you won’t even be around to hear it! Not worth it.

entries.title: A Sibling Is Not Always a ‘Gift’
entries.summary: The term assumes that adding a child to a family is for the best. But that’s not the case for everyone.
entries.content:
The term assumes that adding a child to a family is for the best. But that’s not the case for everyone.

Within months of having her first child, Samantha Savran began hearing from family and friends that she should have a second. Doing so would be the greatest “gift” that she and her husband could give their son, people told them.

At first, Savran agreed. Growing up with a brother, she had liked having a live-in playmate and confidant. But the more she thought about her situation, she grew hesitant. Her birth experience had been traumatic. And she wasn’t sure if having a sibling would be the best for her son, who was thriving. What she and her husband could offer him—Montessori preschool, a family trip to Japan—might not be possible with a second child. But she also knew that sibling relationships could turn painful. In adulthood, her connection with her brother had splintered. They had disagreements that had spiraled into a full-blown falling out, and their relationship was now “difficult,” she told me. “It’s hard to say that I still see it as a ‘gift.’”

The notion that parents should give children a sibling is common. “Life Is Better With Siblings,” declared the headline on a recent New York Times op-ed by the Catholic University professor Catherine Pakaluk, who argued that, unlike small families, “large families generate moral education the way an engine generates heat.” In a column last year for The Guardian, a writer explained that she had “gifted my daughters each other,” and that doing so was a way of “quietly healing my childhood loneliness.” On social media, heartstring-tugging posts of small children holding hands and nuzzling underscore the point: “A baby brother is the universe’s way of giving a little girl her first real love story,” one mom captioned a video.

When I asked online about this kind of messaging, I heard from dozens of parents who had been on the receiving end. A New York City woman who works in health care, fresh off maternity leave, said a patient had told her that she would be “selfish” not to have a second child. Scarlet de Lemeny, a recently married retail consultant based in Boston, told me that before she’d even set a wedding date, people had advised her to have multiple children—because “they need a friend.” This month, the British celebrity Kate Lawler, who has one 5-year-old, wrote in Metro: “I’m now regularly hounded with abuse when I talk about the positives of having just one, as if raising my daughter without a sibling is the cruellest thing I could possibly do.” This prodding isn’t limited to one-child parents. A mother of two boys told me that she keeps hearing she should “definitely try for a third, so you can have a girl.”

The people who implore women to have more kids usually mean well. It’s lovely, and reasonable, to hope that a sibling might become a child’s lifelong friend and source of support. But the “gift” messaging isn’t always benign. For parents, it can add pressure, guilt, and anxiety to an already huge life decision—particularly for women, who in addition to giving birth tend to bear the brunt of fertility expectations, care responsibilities, and mental and physical health burdens, and to take a hit to their long-term employment and earnings prospects.

The “gift” phrasing also rests on a shaky premise. People, after all, aren’t inanimate objects. They are unpredictable beings with a will and their own motivations. And not even the best of intentions can guarantee that a child will experience a new sibling as a gift.

The sibling bond can be unlike any other. I’ve heard people describe their siblings as their “first phone call,” their “life raft,” their “village.” Some siblings can finish one another’s sentences or seem to sense when something is wrong even when they’re far away, in another state. One of my friends is so close with her brother that he made her the “best ma’am” at his wedding. Another person told me that, when her parents kicked her out, her sister took her in—the same weekend the sister was getting married.

Broadly, research shows that sibling relationships tend to be more positive than negative. One large, recent U.S. survey found that more than half of respondents ages 25 to 35 had “tight-knit” relationships with their full siblings. Although events such as starting their own family can cause siblings to drift apart, they typically experience a “rebound,” the sibling researcher Megan Gilligan, an associate professor at the University of Missouri, told me. In one study, a sample of older adults found that most reported warm, low-conflict sibling ties.

But these bonds can be uniquely complicated. “Sibling relationships are different than our other family ties, and they tend to be more complex,” Gilligan said. “We use the term ambivalence: They can be both very positive and very negative, simultaneously.” The same factors that can make these relationships go so right—growing up together; knowing one another’s triggers, foibles, and flaws—can also make them go very wrong. When aging parents need care or die, for instance, their grown children might find benefits to sharing the costs, decision making, and emotional burden, Gilligan said. But in some families, the same situations can cause conflict and resentment.

Research also indicates that it isn’t simply having a sibling that benefits children—it’s having a good relationship with one. That may sound like plain common sense, but the distinction is crucial. A paper last year identified sibling aggression and abuse as “invisible and widespread public health problems.” One watershed 2013 study found that children who endured sibling aggression, including name-calling and “mean” comments, had worse mental health than those who didn’t.

Still darker and less discussed is sibling sexual abuse. There’s no way to know how common it is, Brad Watts, a Tennessee-based therapist who specializes in sibling abuse, told me. But in more than a decade of working with affected families, he has seen a theme: No family is guaranteed immunity. “It can happen in my home,” he told me. “It can happen in anybody’s home.”

Watts has three boys. He has loved watching them become close friends. But he would never tell someone to “give” their child a sibling. “I can talk about all kinds of siblings that were not ‘gifts,’” Watts said. “They were, more or less, terrors.” Even close sibling relationships aren’t always beneficial. Studies over the years have found that adolescents are more likely to engage in risky behavior, such as smoking or unsafe sex, and even to break the law if another sibling did—especially if their relationship is tight.

Calling a younger sibling a “gift” can create unintended consequences, too, Whitney Goodman, a Miami-based therapist, told me. Although this is surely no one’s intent, the phrasing can imply that a child has been brought into the world in the service of another. The parental preference it suggests may cause children to feel they’re treated or desired differently—one of the most common reasons sibling relationships fracture.

Learning to navigate life with someone you didn’t choose to grow up with can be rewarding. But not always. The same large U.S. survey that found “tight-knit” relationships among many full siblings also found that up to one in five sibling relationships were characterized by “detachment”—meaning that siblings were less likely to have frequent contact, to feel emotionally close, or to offer one another social or financial support. In Germany, researchers looking at a nationally representative sample of nearly 6,000 adults found that 28 percent of respondents were estranged from a sibling at least once over the study’s six-year period.

De Lemeny, the Boston retail consultant, has amassed more than half a million followers across TikTok and Instagram by sharing about her life and childhood, and her experience going no-contact with her parents. Many followers ask about her brother, assuming that they must have “trauma-bonded.” When she explains that, actually, she and her brother don’t speak, some are shocked. Others thank her: They weren’t close to their siblings and thought they were alone in this. “It’s a dynamic that doesn’t really get spoken about,” de Lemeny said. “It’s something that carries a lot of shame.”

This silence about conflict and estrangement can have ripple effects in the broader culture. It might lead parents-to-be to assume that, barring some grave unlikelihood, siblings will be friends for life. It also contributes to the narrative that if a person doesn’t “give” their child a sibling, they will be, unequivocally, depriving them of something important.

Anna de Sapio, a social worker in the United Kingdom, gave birth during the first COVID lockdown and struggled with isolation, exhaustion, and postpartum depression and anxiety. Yet when her daughter was only four months old, de Sapio began to get the question: When are you planning to give her a sibling? It made de Sapio feel “depleted,” she told me—as if, no matter how much of herself she gave, it wasn’t enough.

Nearly every mother I spoke with expressed guilt about her decision making: one-child moms for not “giving” their child a built-in best friend; multiple-child moms who after having additional kids felt awful that they had less time and attention for their first. And these days, the pressure is coming not just from friends and family but also from politicians and other public figures: Donald Trump floating “baby bonuses”; Elon Musk arguing that the “number one threat to the West” is low birth rates; tradwives, tech bros, and other proponents of the pronatalist movement who repeat over and over that having more children isn’t a lifestyle choice—it’s a moral good.

Like the “moral good” rhetoric, which assumes that having more babies is all upside, the “gift” rhetoric ignores the fact that having one child may simply be the best decision for many families—including for solo children. Research spanning decades suggests that, contrary to stereotype, only children tend to be just as well-adjusted as kids in multi-child households, enjoy the same or better mental health, and have closer relationships with their parents. They are no more narcissistic, competitive, or lonely than those with siblings. And although they may possess, as very young children, slightly-less-developed interpersonal skills, these differences generally disappear over time.

Plus, let’s be blunt: Regardless of how much parents love every child that they have, additional children can add stress and expense. This can affect the mental well-being of parents and, by extension, their children. Kids generally fare better when their caregivers are in good mental health, can invest more time in caregiving, and are sensitive and responsive to their child’s needs. These nuances may help explain why, on average, children with more than three or four siblings have worse mental and physical health than kids with fewer or none.

The “gift” phrasing misses something else, too: When people frame siblings as gifts and being an only child as a deficit, they discount what many only-child families told me they’ve experienced: the joy that can come from having a small, tight-knit family where jealousies and conflicts are mostly absent, and parents’ time and attention are undivided.

After several years of uncertainty, Savran and her husband made a decision: They would stick to having one child. “Giving the best life we can to the one kid we have,” she said, “and making sure he’s surrounded by friends and ‘framily’ and people who love him, ended up being our priority.” No one knows what a sibling might bring. But this kind of careful decision making—which takes the capacities, joys, and temperaments of already existing family members into account—can be its own gift.

entries.title: A Trojan Horse Is Supposed to Have Humans Inside It
entries.summary: Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey is full of contradictions about deceit and violence.
entries.content:
Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey is full of contradictions about deceit and violence.

If you go to Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, you may be able to purchase, for a mere $69.99, a plastic receptacle shaped as a Trojan horse. The horse is used in the film as an image of moral decline. But the repurposing of a sinister instrument of war into a popcorn container hints at the malleability of the conceit: A Trojan horse contains unexpected multitudes.

This mythical item has always been a tricky symbol, used by generations of storytellers and artists to map shifting perceptions of deception in war. The physical design of Nolan’s version is striking and wildly out of keeping with earlier representations, including ancient depictions and the pull-toy design of the giant equine in Wolf Petersen’s fun 2004 blockbuster, Troy. Nolan’s horse rears upright rather than standing on four hooves. The unwieldy creature is discovered half-buried in the sand, and proves almost impossible for the Trojans to lug into the city. This cinematic prop is an extraordinary feat of engineering: It stands nearly 40 feet tall and took hundreds of people to drag up the beach. The physical horror of people being trapped inside as the seawater rises is brilliantly and terrifyingly evoked.

But on a narrative level, Nolan’s horse is light as air. In comparison with other blockbusters—such as, say, the Die Hard films, also action-packed tales of one man’s dangerous journey back to his wife—The Odyssey contains far more pontificating about values and civilizational decline, but much less coherence and less heart. It gestures at a critique of xenophobia and violence, but it focuses primarily on the perspective of the guilty, traumatized warrior rather than that of his victims. Moreover, the movie’s devoted attention to mechanics, and its heedless willingness to give us massacres as spectacle, undermines its moralizing claims of caring about man’s inhumanity to man. Verbally, we are told that people matter; visually, we are shown that they do not.

In ancient myth, Troy was a wealthy, powerful city whose walls were built by two gods, Apollo and Poseidon. Such walls could never be breached by mere mortals. So when Greek warriors gathered to besiege the city and retrieve the wife and wealth stolen from the Spartan king Menelaus by the Trojan prince Paris, they found themselves at an impasse: The great army, unable to break through Troy’s divinely constructed defenses, remained immobilized on the beach for 10 years.

Things changed only when Athena, the daughter of Zeus and goddess of military strategy, put an idea into the mind of her favorite mortal, Odysseus: to instruct the master craftsman Epeius to build a massive, hollow horse, inside which Odysseus and the other Greeks could hide. Odysseus was, as Nolan obviously recognizes, a mythical Robert Oppenheimer: a hero able to devise the ultimate weapon that could end a seemingly unwinnable war.

We do not know who first told the story of the Trojan horse, but it was in circulation by at least the early seventh century B.C.E. The earliest extant artistic depiction is on a large storage jar (in Greek called a pithos) from the island of Mykonos. It features a long-legged horse that has square cutout windows for the warriors to be seen through; outside the horse, more fighters are enslaving terrified women and children. The image is, like the popcorn-bucket horse, a joke: It would ruin the trick if the horse had windows.

The Homeric Odyssey, along with The Iliad and the poems of Hesiod, were likely composed around roughly the same time as the making of the Trojan-horse pithos, using the new technology that had become available in the Greek-speaking world in the mid-eighth century B.C.E.: the alphabet. This development enabled one or more composers—“Homer”—to create and preserve monumental written poems based on the oral tales about the great, lost days of heroes—characters who did extraordinary things and were closer to the gods than any normal mortal. The myths included partial, fictionalized folk memories of the earlier period of Greek prosperity, when the Mycenaeans built palatial structures and formed extensive trade routes across the eastern Mediterranean and beyond. Homer’s Odyssey draws on many generations of preexisting myth but reshapes the old stories for its own era—a time of migration, colonization, urbanization, political and social diversity, and technological change.

In The Odyssey, Odysseus repeatedly finds new ways to reenact his most famous trick of hiding inside the horse (an assumed backstory not described in the main narrative). He hides in the care of Calypso (whose name suggests “hiding”), beneath the name of No Man, under the sheep of Polyphemus, and in the guise of an old beggar. Eventually, he replicates his triumph at Troy in his own house by technological mastery of another trick involving a wooden weapon (this time, his bow). Odysseus’s mastery of technology enables him to invade a heavily defended home in disguise, achieve an impossible victory, and break an impasse, answering the long-deferred question of which man will claim the household and Penelope as his bride.

In one of only two extensive passages in Homer that evoke the horse explicitly (a long episode that Nolan excises), Odysseus, while enjoying the lavish hospitality of the Phaeacians on Scheria, asks a blind poet to sing the story of the Trojan horse. The poet complies, and Odysseus weeps at the story of his greatest triumph. The narrator offers a surprising simile: Odysseus sobs “as pitifully as a woman weeps” while watching her warrior husband die in a failed attempt to defend his city and his children. The woman falls desperately on her dying husband, but his killers are behind her, hitting her with spears as they force her into a life of enslavement. The simile suggests a connection between the victorious Odysseus and the victims of his greatest success. We are not told whether Odysseus is crying because he feels guilt and pity at the thought of those he has killed, tricked, and enslaved, or because he is tormented to be trapped so far away from either the battlefield or Ithaca—the spheres where he can be honored and known. The scene is a memorable reminder that warfare has victims as well as victors, and that it may sometimes be difficult to tell which is which.

After many misadventures, and eight years in the beds of two different goddesses, Odysseus makes it home from eastern Troy to western Ithaca. He is able to move from what Homer’s contemporary Hesiod calls the brutal “age of bronze” and the glorious “age of heroes” into the conflict-ridden “age of iron,” because he has mastered not only warfare with bronze weapons but also the more social skills of rhetoric, cunning, and technology—skills that enable him to survive and win eternal glory, even when he is far from the battlefield. Homer’s Odysseus specializes in clever scheming—in Greek, mētis—and the narrator does not invite us to moralize against a flexible relationship with the truth.

Many centuries later, Virgil set his Roman epic, The Aeneid, in the aftermath of the Trojan War, and modeled its narrative on both The Odyssey and The Iliad. The protagonist, Aeneas, is like Odysseus in that he is a warrior on a journey from Troy to his western homeland. But whereas Odysseus returns to his original home, Aeneas is a migrant Trojan, fleeing his fallen city for a new homeland to which he has never been: Italy, where he will begin the historical process that is fated, one day, to lead to the foundation of the glorious city of Rome. Virgil reinvents the story of Odysseus in a double way. Homer’s hero becomes both the pious refugee, Aeneas, and the cruel liar, Ulysses (the Roman name for Odysseus), who destroys a city through his unscrupulous wiles.

Homer leaves the Trojans to decide for themselves whether to take the horse into the city. But Virgil adds a character who persuades them to do so: Sinon, a cousin of “cruel Ulysses,” who shares his penchant for lies. Sinon, whose name means “harmer,” is found bound and alone after the Greeks pretend to sail away. He tells the Trojans a pitiful story about how he barely escaped being sacrificed by Ulysses, claiming that the horse is an offering specifically for Athena (Minerva in Latin), who will ensure the city’s salvation if they take the horse inside. Yielding to their pious respect for the gods, and their eagerness to show mercy toward vulnerable suppliants, the Trojans free Sinon from his bonds and take the deadly horse inside their city. Aeneas, who narrates the story to the Carthaginian queen Dido, comments (in the translation by Scott McGill and Susannah Wright):

His tactics and the tears he falsely shed

now captured us—we who had not been beaten

by Tydides, Thessalian Achilles,

ten years of warfare, or a thousand ships.

The addition of Sinon makes it clear that deception happens not primarily through inanimate mechanical objects but through people deliberately using rhetoric to manipulate audiences, and through the choices of those audiences about what and whom to believe. With the Sinon episode, Virgil asks his readers to consider whether cities and civilizations may fall for noble motives rather than because of moral failures.

Virgil’s version of the Trojan-horse episode was written in the time of the first Roman emperor, Augustus. The new leader was a canny manipulator of words and imagery who presented his revolutionary autocratic regime as if it were in line with Roman tradition. Virgil showcases the dangers of deception and offers an account of how easily good people can be deceived. The scene offers an ambivalent reflection on the culture and politics of its time. We might read Sinon’s deceptions in light of his Greekness: Perhaps the future Roman people need fear no such schemes, as long as they hold fast to their own identity and maintain suspicion of all foreigners, especially Greeks. But we can also see a dark shadow in Augustus’s manipulation of the Roman people through clever storytelling that disguised and enabled the destruction of the old Republic and the slide into one-man rule.

Where Virgil’s Ulysses is cruel and predatory, and his mendacious instrument, Sinon, is unambiguously a bad guy, Nolan re-creates Sinon as his film’s sinless moral center. The focus on “sin” is presumably the reason for the odd but consistent pronunciation of the name: More normally pronounced by English-speakers as Sigh-non or See-non—echoing the long i of the Latin—in Nolan’s film, it’s always Sin-none as if to reinforce the Christlike innocence of Elliot Page’s version of the classical “harmer.” Nolan’s Sinon is not a trickster but a poor innocent to whom Odysseus has lied by omission, in failing to tell him about the trick with the horse. The episode is a cautionary fable about a director who fails to trust an actor to play his part: Odysseus lies so that Sinon will give the most convincing possible performance when he falsely tells the Trojans, with his dying breath, that the horse is a gift.

The film’s oft-invoked “Zeus’s law” is explained as a version of the Golden Rule: We must host beggars and strangers kindly, to “do as we would be done by,” and because they could be gods in disguise (a quite different point). The unkindness of Penelope’s suitors to Odysseus’s poor dog Argos and to the blind Eumaeus is a clear violation of this principle. Yet the film also suggests that the law of Zeus is concerned with a quite different moral problem: deception. The horse is presented as the ultimate violation of the law of Zeus, because it entails wielding a weapon of mass destruction disguised as a gift. The Homeric Zeus is a cunning schemer, whereas Nolan’s Zeus takes a particularly hard line on deceit, especially in relationships between hosts and guests. The film’s arch-villain, the lead suitor, Antinous, proves his villainy by being a bad guest, and a bad host, and an entertainingly weaselly liar. The horse is presented as breaking “civilization” because it represents the moment when the good guy, Odysseus, echoes the behavior of the bad guy by being a deceitful, ungrateful guest. But the film does not explain what “hospitality” has to do with a narrative situation in which the Greeks have been besieging Troy for 10 years already; the Trojans are not their hosts but their enemies in war. If the war is bad, it is nonsensical to suggest that the most important turning point is the use of the horse rather than Agamemnon’s choice to invade Troy in the first place and Odysseus’s choice to yield to the empire’s demands. The visually impressive spectacle of the horse on a stunning stretch of pristine beach (shot in Essaouira, Morocco) contributes to the narrative muddle: The Greeks have supposedly been encamped there for the past decade, yet it shows no sign of human habitation.

Nolan shot the Calypso episodes in the disputed Moroccan-occupied territory of Western Sahara without the consent of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. The choice underlines the lack of seriousness in Nolan’s thinking about his themes: the ethical and cultural costs of entering other people’s homes uninvited, for the purpose of extracting resources without respect for an unwilling host.

In Homer, deception is relatively benign. In Virgil, it is evil. But in both poems, we learn directly about how the Greeks enacted their schemes, as well as the decision-making process of the pious, thoughtful Trojans. In Nolan, we never see Odysseus planning the construction of the horse or lying to the innocent Sinon, and his Trojans take mere seconds to make up their minds. The film is not interested in the social or psychological questions of how people deceive and are deceived. Deception is a fait accompli: The horse appears on the beach in the opening sequence as if deposited there by helicopter, and Sinon does not know that he is not telling the truth. What matters cinematically are the logistics: the rolling of the horse uphill and the claustrophobic, waterlogged interior. Once the ambush of the Trojans begins, the camera lingers repeatedly not on the human actors but on the enflamed, toppling buildings and the great gates of the city, whose slow-moving mechanism is observed at great length. The script tells us loudly that people matter, but the camera shows us that what matters is the mechanical challenge of moving objects through space.

Nolan’s Odysseus goes to war to protect his biological son, Telemachus, but in so doing betrays his quasi-son, Sinon—an irony whose emotional impact is dulled by the film’s frenetic pacing. Page is a luminous, heartbreaking presence on-screen, whereas the Trojans are mostly masked nonentities. Odysseus’s moral development is retold in miniature on the island of Circe, where he shoots what he thinks is an animal but then realizes was actually a human being. Yet neither Odysseus nor the film itself seems to move beyond the occasional moment or two of noticing the humanity of all humans. The face of the slaughtered deer-man is not shown, and the film’s narrative rushes on. The final massacre of the cartoonishly bestial suitors inside Odysseus’s house is presented with thrilling exuberance, and the camera does not linger on the pain and humanity of those who die or allow for the possibility that they, too, should be mourned. Instead, the long, repetitive final fight sequence fixates, again, on logistics: how the weapons are hidden, and how they descend from the storeroom through a hole in the ceiling. The film’s primary fascination with maneuvering objects creates a mismatch between what we see and what we are being told to think and feel. We see inside the horse, but we do not see inside the characters or their world.

In the final sequence of the movie, Odysseus leaves home for yet another journey. It draws heavily on Alfred Tennyson’s poem Ulysses, whose narrator abandons his “agèd wife” and leaves his son, Telemachus, on the throne of Ithaca, while he departs for the “untravell’d world” “to follow knowledge like a sinking star.” Matt Damon as Odysseus likewise embarks in a boat toward the sunset, although he gets to take his wife (played by Anne Hathaway) along for the ride. The self-imposed exile of Odysseus enables his son (Tom Holland) to rule over the Ithacans who survive. The camera depicts the newly becrowned prince as a sunlit golden boy, who can receive the power and wealth won by his father’s bloody hands without having to taint his own—although we have been given no reason to believe that Telemachus is ready for the role, or that the concentration of power and wealth in one man is beneficial for anyone.

The final goal of Nolan’s Odysseus is not infinite knowledge but redemption: He is at last awake from his amnesia and intends to bury the comrades left uninterred on his journeys. Yet the waking vision of the protagonist, and hence also of the film, remains extraordinarily narrow. There is no suggestion that he will offer burial to the Trojans, or the suitors, or the various foreigners killed during his journey. Despite Odysseus’s spiritual awakening, the dead remain as dead as ever. But there is a spectacular sunset and yet another lavish display of a large vehicle grandly making its way through space, across churning waves.

Nolan’s Odyssey is itself a kind of Trojan horse. The script grandly insists on the importance of human kindness, while the camera shows us an entirely different set of values. In these times of hatred and misinformation, we need more than the “apparent magic” of deceptive images. We need art that is truthful about the costs and the necessity of compassion, and that recognizes that a sense of spiritual superiority may not protect us from lies. These lessons are legible in Homer and Virgil, but are elided by Nolan’s visually stunning, emotionally empty film.

entries.title: The Catholic Church’s New Schism
entries.summary: The Vatican excommunicated 700 arch-traditionalist bishops and priests—a rupture that touches on broader disputes in the Church today.
entries.content:
The Vatican excommunicated 700 arch-traditionalist bishops and priests—a rupture that touches on broader disputes in the Church today.

At an open-air Mass in Écône, Switzerland, before a crowd of about 16,000 people, four priests became bishops last month. The men professed their fidelity to tradition against “heretics, schismatics, and those who rebel against our Holy Father.” They did so knowing full well that, in becoming bishops, they lacked something the Catholic Church deems essential: permission from the pope.

All four of these men are members of the Society of Saint Pius X, or SSPX, an arch-traditionalist group of clergy founded in 1970 by the French archbishop Marcel Lefebvre. For decades, SSPX has battled with the Vatican over the group’s fear that, as one theologian told me, “in reading the signs of the times, the Catholic Church is more beholden to the times than she is a light to the nations.” Now tensions have reached a breaking point.

The Vatican warned SSPX before the Écône Mass that consecrating bishops without a papal mandate would be considered a “schismatic act,” a formal separation from the Catholic Church. After the Mass, the Church issued a decree saying that the new bishops, plus the two who ordained them, incurred an automatic excommunication: They can neither receive communion nor celebrate licit Masses nor officiate valid marriages and confessions. The 700 or so SSPX priests worldwide will also fall into schism, and thereby be excommunicated, if they remain with the society. Even lay churchgoers who “formally adhere” to the group may face the same sanction.

By some estimates, 25,000 people in the United States are affiliated with SSPX—a tiny fraction of the roughly 53 million American Catholic adults. Many Catholics may not even know that the Church finds itself in arguably its largest schism since the 19th century. Nonetheless, the SSPX excommunications touch on broader disputes in Catholicism today: about reform, orthodoxy, and whether the Church’s institutional changes of the past half century have been for the better. That is, this schism is about more than just SSPX. It’s also about how the Church will respond to a larger group of traditionalists—those who, though still Catholic, have questioned or even attacked many of the beliefs and practices that characterize the faith today.

SSPX’s fight with the Catholic Church began as a response to the Second Vatican Council, or Vatican II, the most pivotal event of 20th-century Catholic history. From 1962 to 1965, the Church instituted a series of reforms that reimagined its role in a secular age. Perhaps most famous was the council’s overhaul of the Mass in hopes of increasing participation among the faithful. In most Masses, priests stopped facing the altar and began facing the people. The local language replaced Latin as the main tongue of worship. In some parishes, out went Gregorian chants and in came guitars.

Vatican II also reformed the doctrine of extra ecclesiam nulla salus, or “outside the Church, there is no salvation.” As Larry Chapp, a former theology professor at DeSales University, told me, the council clarified that Catholics “have to be open to the movement of grace outside of the boundaries of the Church.” Guided by this vision, Vatican II produced writings that promoted religious freedom, ecumenical efforts with other Christians, and “dialogue and collaboration” with non-Christian religions.

To SSPX, these changes were calamitous. The society’s 28-page profession of faith asserts that true Catholicism rejects ecumenical and interfaith dialogue, and states that other faiths are “false religions” and “the work of the devil.” SSPX also holds fast to the pre–Vatican II Traditional Latin Mass as the only legitimate liturgy: The profession of faith declares that the vernacular Mass “favours heresy, weakens the faith,” and “turns the faithful away from the adoration due to God.”

Lefebvre participated in Vatican II himself—he even signed all of the writings that SSPX now objects to. But he soon started denouncing the council’s reforms. Five years after the council concluded, he founded SSPX with the mission of training priests in preconciliar beliefs and practices. In 1974, Lefebvre condemned Vatican II for contributing to “the destruction of the Church,” one of the many accusations and acts of defiance that prompted Church authorities to revoke his permission to run the society. Lefebvre kept recruiting priests anyway. By 1988, SSPX had approximately 200 clergy worldwide, mainly in France, Switzerland, and the United States. In June of that year, Lefebvre ordained four priests as bishops, ignoring Pope John Paul II’s orders not to. The pontiff excommunicated Lefebvre and the four bishops but declared no formal schism. Lefebvre, for his part, continued leading the society—and vehemently opposing Vatican II, which he described as the “adulterous marriage of the Church with liberal ideas”—until his death in 1991.

The Vatican let SSPX exist in a kind of limbo state in the years after the 1988 excommunications. Members of the society were officially limited in the sacraments that they could officiate, but SSPX kept ordaining priests and holding illicit Masses. And yet they were still, technically, a part of the Catholic Church. Church leaders, Chapp said, made “efforts to bring them back into the fold.” In 2009, Pope Benedict XVI lifted the excommunications of the four living SSPX bishops that John Paul II had effected two decades prior. A few years later, Pope Francis granted SSPX priests permission to hear confessions and officiate marriages. Still, SSPX has no interest in being part of a Church that doesn’t spurn Vatican II. The society holds that the council’s reforms create a “state of necessity” that allows it to do what it must “to preserve the faith.” This is the irony at the heart of SSPX’s theology: The society claims to be a bulwark of the Catholic faith; it also dismisses the pope’s authority as the final interpreter of that faith. “This is not a trivial issue,” Chapp said. “Staying in union with the vicar of Christ is a central defining feature of what it means to be Catholic.”

Although SSPX considers itself a lone defender of tradition, other prominent Catholics—including popes—have expressed concerns about the liturgy and emphasized the importance of doctrinal clarity. Before his pontificate, Pope Benedict XVI worried that Vatican II’s liturgical changes, as implemented, had in some situations downplayed the “authentic inner vibrancy” of the Mass. John Paul II was a consistent proponent of interfaith dialogue, but nonetheless cautioned in 1990 against “a religious relativism which leads to the belief that ‘one religion is as good as another.’”

But these popes—and many other Catholics who have raised questions about the implementation of certain Church reforms—were working within the Church, not against it. SSPX, by contrast, “doesn’t have to wrestle with unclarity or ambiguity,” Father Gregory Pine, a professor of moral theology at the Dominican House of Studies in Washington, D.C., told me. It doesn’t do the hard theological work of interpreting new teachings alongside tradition. It simply maintains a posture of rejection—and calls it orthodoxy.

It’s one thing for a tiny sect to go rogue. But traditionalism has many supporters in the broader Catholic Church—which means that how the Church moves forward has implications not only for SSPX but also for this larger set of traditionalists, and for the unity of the Church as a whole.

Like SSPX, some traditionalists have been viciously critical of the pope, especially during Francis’s pontificate. On a 2024 visit to Singapore, for example, the late pontiff met with an interfaith group of youth and said that “all religions are paths to God”—an off-the-cuff comment that reflected a Vatican II teaching that non-Christian religions “often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all.” Still, several prominent Catholic traditionalists denounced Francis. One said that he spouted “heresy that flies in the face of Jesus Christ.” Another created a video titled “Pope Francis Is a Heretic Denying Tradition, Part 2” that echoed arguments SSPX had made before. The Traditional Latin Mass also has a following beyond SSPX. Roughly 1 million American Catholic adults attend it weekly, which is just 2 percent of the country’s overall Catholic adult population but still many more people than are affiliated with the society.

The SSPX excommunications contain a clear message to all traditionalists: Vatican II itself is not up for debate. The council’s teachings and reforms are essential components of the faith, not optional addenda to it. Some Catholics believe that the Church should also continue its official position of limiting access to the Traditional Latin Mass. The Catholic writer Mike Lewis told me that support for the liturgy tends to come with an “entire theological structure” that questions the authority of Vatican II and, by extension, the pope.

Father Pine, however, said that some proponents of the Traditional Latin Mass are simply looking for a liturgy that is “celebrated worthily” and at a “transcendent register.” And some Church leaders have signaled an openness to the Traditional Latin Mass in the weeks since the excommunications. Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone—whom Pope Leo XIV recently appointed to the Vatican’s highest court—has called for “more access” to the liturgy, and some U.S. bishops have promoted it as part of their pleas to SSPX’s followers to return to the Church.

Leo XIV has stressed unity since he became pope, last year, and he has not made his position on the Traditional Latin Mass fully known. In excommunicating SSPX, he rebuked a small group of the most vocal supporters of the Traditional Latin Mass. But he has also met with a well-known proponent of the liturgy, as well as with the authors of a forthcoming book that argues that Traditional Latin Mass–goers aren’t the recalcitrants their critics make them out to be.

Excommunication, the theologians I spoke with told me, serves a dual purpose: It’s punitive, but it’s also medicinal, meant to call a person or group back to communion. SSPX’s lay members, by early indications, plan to remain in schism for the time being. Those who return, though, may well find their Church to be a bit more open to traditionalism than they imagined it would be.

entries.title: One Problem With Attacking the Smithsonian? Americans Like It.
entries.summary: Coming after a history museum may not be the base-galvanizing issue Trump thinks it is.
entries.content:
Coming after a history museum may not be the base-galvanizing issue Trump thinks it is.

Earlier this year, I visited a “Freedom Truck,” one of the patriotic mobile museums that the Trump administration is sending around the country for the nation’s 250 birthday. There, I had a wide-ranging conversation with a visitor who complained that the U.S. education system is not teaching what she called true history. But when I mentioned the Smithsonian, her disposition changed entirely. She’d heard rumors about “a lot of liberalism going through the Smithsonian now,” she told me, but added, “I love the Smithsonian. I don’t have a problem with it.”

I hear this a lot, actually. Even now, as the museum complex continues to face a pressure campaign from the White House, public fondness for the Smithsonian—for its free entry and eclectic collections—is hard to break among those otherwise receptive to President Trump’s anti-institutionalism.

Attacks on the credibility of institutions, especially those that disseminate information—universities, public schools, media organizations—have become commonplace in this so-called post-truth age. Recent data from Gallup, published last month, suggested that confidence in the majority of institutions asked about in the survey, including newspapers, public schools, and TV news, is at or near historic lows. Pollsters, meanwhile, don’t even include museums in the Gallup surveys. Although museums have certainly faced some criticism from the left and right, until now, they’ve been largely immune to the most deleterious effects of the culture wars.

This may be because most Americans, unlike the president, seem to trust these entities to do their thing. A YouGov survey last week found that 57 percent of Americans said that the amount of influence the president should have over exhibits and programming at federally funded museums should be “none” or “not much.” Just 17 percent of Republicans seemed to take the president’s position: that he should have a “great deal” of influence. Coming after a history museum may not be the base-galvanizing issue the White House hopes it is.

Industry data support these findings. In a survey this year, Wilkening Consulting, in partnership with the American Alliance of Museums, found that when people were asked whether museums, faced with pressure, should remove content on topics such as slavery and climate change, the majority of conservatives (63 percent) and liberals (83 percent) disagreed. An oft-cited statistic from the same pair of organizations places museums among the most trusted sources of information in American life, falling just behind public libraries and family and friends. It suggests that museums occupy a rare and cozy place in the collective imagination.

At a time of high mistrust in not just institutions but also observable reality, people seem to still find a sense of stability in these keepers of public memory. Perhaps it makes sense that Americans would put their last bits of trust in the very places that show them what is physically, tangibly real.

For more than a year, the White House has threatened and criticized the Smithsonian, accusing it of spreading divisive narratives and failing to adequately celebrate American history. In recent weeks, the administration has zeroed in on the National Museum of American History, publishing a lengthy report last month decrying exhibits, calling out staff members, and asserting that the museum has fallen victim to “ideological capture” at the hands of a “radical, activist cohort.” During a pair of congressional hearings, the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, attested to her love of this country some half a dozen times while maintaining that telling the American story in all of its complexity is a form of respect for its people.

Two days later, Trump announced an executive order that would effectively plaster untrustworthy on signs outside the National Museum of American History, like an explicit content label on a CD. The administration ordered the National Park Service to put up the signage in front of the museum to correct what it claims is “inaccurate information” and to share the findings of its report, which claims that the current leadership of the Smithsonian and the history museum cannot be trusted to tell the American story.

Right-wing media organizations have echoed this messaging, and since the hearings, Fox News has published dozens of clips and articles criticizing the Smithsonian and scrutinizing its leadership’s pay, highlighting months-old proposed budget cuts, and tallying the number of “liberal items” in a recent exhibit.

The Smithsonian, which is partially government-funded, has faced partisan flare-ups over the years. A controversy over how to display the airplane that dropped the atomic bomb over Hiroshima compelled a museum director to resign in 1995. In 2010, Smithsonian leadership removed from the walls of the National Portrait Gallery an artwork showing a crucifix with ants crawling on it after a right-wing outcry. But these incidents involved single exhibits. Now the White House is making a much more comprehensive case against an entire museum and the institution to which it belongs. With the ordered signs, which will direct visitors to Trump-preferred sources of information, the White House is stepping between visitors and historic objects as though to say: Don’t trust what you see inside. Choose us instead.

This is where museums and friends and family actually share something in common. Culture wars thrive on the unknown. But museums are an in-person activity. “It’s you directly with that artwork or you directly with that specimen, whatever it is. That object feels like it’s speaking directly to you as a trustworthy thing from the past. That in and of itself lends a lot of credibility,” Susie Wilkening, who runs the American Alliance of Museums’ research about museums and trust, told me. Max van Balgooy, a professor of museum studies at the George Washington University, had similar thoughts: “If you see the gun that John Wilkes Booth used or the chair sat in by John Hancock, you’re sort of faced with the truth,” he told me. “You can’t argue with the real stuff.”

Museums weren’t always the hubs of knowledge they are today. They had to both differentiate themselves from the likes of P. T. Barnum’s “museum” as serious scholarly enterprises, devoid of exaggeration and fakes, and invite in ordinary visitors.

At the National Museum of History and Technology, which opened in 1964 and went on to become the National Museum of American History, curators strived not just to show objects but also to tell stories, enhanced with well-designed spaces. In the early days, these stories largely celebrated technological progress: When Daniel Boorstin started as the history museum’s director, in 1969, he nodded to the political ruptures of the era and said, “Here, we emphasize the positive. Without denying our failures, we underline and dramatize our successes.” But as more academics joined the museum, they began to stress questions of who, exactly, benefited from American progress, and worked other critical themes into exhibits. The trend—moving from the rah-rah to the sober—was exemplified by a 1987 exhibition that commemorated the bicentennial of the American Constitution and detailed the abuses of Japanese American internment camps.

Unlike with other kinds of institutions, such as news sites, naysayers can’t easily form museum alternatives aligned with their perspective. (Partisan museums often struggle to compete with mainstream institutions in terms of historical artifacts.) Part of a museum’s trustworthiness may simply come down to the basic fact that it owns these objects and shows them in an authoritative-looking building. Darryl Hart, a history professor at Hillsdale College, an institution that has worked with the Trump administration on education topics, suggested that museumgoers typically don’t think to critique what they see. “For some people, it’s simply part of what they do on a vacation, and I think they check a box,” he told me. “My sense is, people really are going there fairly innocently, not looking for an agenda.”

The data concur. “On the whole, museums are not believed by the American public to have a political agenda,” Colleen Dilenschneider, the founder of Impacts Experience, a market-research firm that examines perceptions of cultural institutions, told me. Her research, which relies on data from the National Awareness, Attitudes, and Usage Study, found that as of July 1, fewer than a quarter of Americans surveyed believed that museums had political agendas—compared with well over half who believed the same of news sources. Liberals and conservatives both overwhelmingly agreed with the statement that museums are “welcoming to people like me.”

Dilenschneider said that “the most shared characteristic of any person in the United States who’s visited a museum in the last year is that they self-identify as a white, non-Hispanic individual” and added that “there are people who are used to hearing their story and they trust that they will continue to hear their story.” Where the story comes from, though, is less clear. Museums contain an essential paradox: They feel transparent because you can walk in and see the work they do. At the same time, the hand behind that work is less visible: As van Balgooy put it, creditless wall texts can read like “the voice of God.”

This impersonal feeling is nearly a definitional feature of institutional trust, Oliver Schilke, the director of the Center for Trust Studies at the University of Arizona, told me. “It’s more a trust in a category of things rather than in specific individuals or counterparts,” he said. This slight distance allows us to form an idealized view on an institution. Putting the spotlight on real people behind it can degrade that trust if they’re being attacked or discredited, as happened during the often-acrimonious Smithsonian hearings last month. At times, lawmakers seemed to be speaking directly to their supporters online, such as when Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina demanded that the history museum’s director tell her whether she believes that men can become women.

When Victoria Cain, a professor at Northeastern University who studies the history of museums and education, described museums’ role in life today, she made them sound like a tonic to the most charged parts of contemporary discourse. Akin to secular churches, museums have taken on a ritualistic quality, she told me: “You can go be in a common space with other people in an act of appreciation.”

In this regard, museums aren’t just a last bastion of public faith—they’re a rare, shared, bipartisan cultural space. These days, many people lament the ways that we have retreated into information silos, full of others who agree with us. But you can’t chop up Thomas Jefferson’s desk and give half of it to the right and half to the left. If we all want to see the desk where the Declaration of Independence was written, we’re going to have to learn, first, to be in the same room.

entries.title: The Danger of Trump’s Anti-Communist Rhetoric
entries.summary: The Trump administration would like you to worry like it’s 1979.
entries.content:
The Trump administration would like you to worry like it’s 1979.

Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.

Karl Marx wrote that political actors often borrow the language and symbols of earlier struggles to wage their own battles. So perhaps he would have been unsurprised to hear the Trump administration resurrect the political rhetoric of the Cold War fight against Marxism.

President Trump, at Wheeler High School in the Atlanta suburbs earlier this summer, mentioned communism or communist 15 times, starting less than a minute into his hour-plus speech: “Communism is the single greatest threat to our country and its history—including even World War I and World War II, Pearl Harbor, 9/11,” he claimed. “I think it’s the greatest threat that I’ve ever seen to our country.”

Last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio convened political leaders, counterterrorism professionals, and law-enforcement officers from 66 countries for what the State Department billed as an extraordinary gathering aimed at confronting “a transnational threat.” From a podium flanked by world flags, Rubio spoke of the need to combat the far left around the world. “This is a distinctive and unique evil,” he said. “They can call themselves anti-capitalist or anti-imperialist or communist or anarchist or Marxist, but the fundamental character is always the same.” The State Department even has a culprit in mind, last week releasing a 100-page report that characterized Cuba as “posing a unique threat” to American security.

Never mind that the island nation of 11 million people lost its chief sponsor with the Soviet Union’s collapse and is so economically strapped that the regime rations electricity and gas. The official line of the U.S. government is that Havana has backed “left-wing terrorism” inside the United States—including “violent BLM militants” and “Antifa terror cells”—and provides a refuge for communism in the Western Hemisphere. “The Cuba that they’re describing, going back to the ’60s and onward, doesn’t exist anymore,” Ted Piccone, a senior foreign-policy adviser for the Clinton administration, told us. “I think they’re just fighting an old ghost in old battles.”

From the standpoint of the White House, however, reviving communism as a boogeyman is a way to tie together two very current objectives. On the home front, experts told us that the vilification of Communists could be an attempt to shift the focus away from painful pocketbook issues such as higher gas prices and inflation, and to paint Democrats, and democratic socialists in particular, as anti-American ahead of the midterms. Overseas, fighting Marxism, especially in Latin America, injects principle into the administration’s desire for dominance in the Western Hemisphere, which so far has led to the removal of a leftist dictator in Venezuela and laid the groundwork for the overthrow of the regime in Havana. Tommy Pigott, a State Department spokesperson, said in a statement that the United States will “not ignore the threat posed by a regime 90 miles off our coast intent on undermining the national security of the American people through espionage and the spread of its failed, insidious ideology.”

Others see less ideological combat, more exercise of American muscle. “The idea is to get rid of any government in the Western Hemisphere that’s not willing to toe the line,” William LeoGrande, a former dean of American University’s School of Public Affairs, told us. “It started with Venezuela, obviously, and now turned to Cuba.” He added, “If I was Daniel Ortega,” Nicaragua’s autocratic ruler, “I might be a little worried that I’d be next.”

U.S. voters may regard the revival of the “Reds under the bed” scare as a desperate attempt by an unpopular president to bolster his party’s election chances. Others may see Rubio using an outdated threat as cover to achieve greater American influence. But the push is already having an effect elsewhere, as other Latin American governments paint pro-democracy protesters as Marxists intent on undermining public order to justify crackdowns.

Trump and his allies have repeatedly described Democrats as socialists or Communists, regardless of how moderate those Democrats’ positions were. During the 2016 presidential campaign, he referred to Senator Bernie Sanders, a democratic socialist, as just a “socialist.” And the October before the 2018 midterms, Trump wrote in an op-ed in USA Today that the “new Democrats are radical socialists” who want to introduce “open-borders socialism,” and he warned that their economic policies were modeled after the socialist policies of Nicolás Maduro’s Venezuela. He never used the word communism, though, and despite his warnings, Democrats took control of the House. By 2024, Trump was calling his rival for the presidency “Comrade Kamala.”

This June, the president again started describing Democratic candidates as “Communist.” Speaking at the Faith & Freedom Coalition’s policy conference, Trump declared: “It’s becoming a communist party. These are not social Democrats; these are hard-core, godless Communists.” A Reuters analysis revealed that Trump invoked the word communism more than 80 times in the two weeks leading up to July 8.

The shift followed primary victories by democratic-socialist candidates in New York, California, and Colorado, as well as last year’s sweeping victory by the DSA standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani to become mayor of New York City. Polls currently suggest that the Democrats could win one or both chambers of Congress in November.

“The Democrats’ full-blown embrace of socialism and communism is a mortal threat to American liberty,” the White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told us in a statement. “President Trump will never allow America to become a socialist or communist country.”

Others in the administration, including Vice President Vance, have echoed Trump’s rhetoric. But no member has been more fervent in his public disdain for Communists than Rubio. His anti-communism is deeply personal. The secretary, the first of Latino descent to serve in the role, is the grandson of Cuban exiles who fled the island as Fidel Castro took power, settling in South Florida, where Rubio grew up. “Marco’s talked about this a lot—growing up in a Cuban American community, you hear the stories: firsthand accounts about repression; about not having basic freedoms; about watching an economy just collapse under that system,” Cesar Conda, Rubio’s former Senate chief of staff, told us. “That stuff shapes you. I think it shaped him, from a really young age.”

That hatred of communism became a constant reprise through Rubio’s career in local and state politics in Florida, in the U.S. Senate, and in the Trump administration. “It’s not complicated once you understand where he comes from,” Conda said. “It’s personal, it’s family, it’s ideology, and yeah, there’s a strategic piece to it, too. But the family history—that’s the big one. That’s really where it starts.”

Rubio does not hold all Communists to the same standard. Conda recalled that Rubio, while a Senator in 2014, “said he’d never wanted to set foot in Communist China” because of his contempt for communist regimes. His criticism of China’s human-rights record put Rubio on a Chinese sanctions list in 2020—twice. (Rubio’s trip to Beijing with Trump this year was his first.) But Rubio told reporters late last month that China, still home to the world’s largest and most successful Communist Party, would remain a diplomatic partner to the United States. “These are the two most powerful economies in the world, two large militaries, two nuclear powers,” Rubio said. “We have to have a relationship with China, and we want it to be as positive as it possibly can be.” (Imagine President Ronald Reagan saying the same about the Soviets.) Rubio has paid relatively little attention to the other nominally left-wing regime in North Korea.

Instead, the administration has depicted Western Europe as a new hotbed of Marxism.
